So, the overall rating here is too low. Don't look at my rating, because my 3 is like a 3.5 here. I might be cotributing to the problem here but come on, fans of this type of post-rock have to enjoy this more. I guess, some people don't like the electronics and want more cheesy dreamscapes with crescendos (though they have one or two here). I haven't listened to anything by the band but this album is quite explorative and adventurous in the overall approach. That said, it is also kinda safe for my liking when it comes to the melodies and the actual music, whatever that means. Certain parts I really enjoy and certain parts sound like a soundtrack to some indie romantic drama (so as much as I hate the cover, it describes certain parts of this album perfectly), which is not a compliment. I mean some parts are pretty in cheese (someone should make a movie with that tile), especially when you have Robert Smith singing. However, focusing on the substance, it has a lot to offer, well at least much more than usually the albums with a 3.16 average do. Like if Battles is a 40 year-old man, this album is that person when he was 16.

I just can't stand the vocals and the music is like a watered-down Drive Like Jehu, which isn't necessarily a bad thing but the vocals just ruin it for me. You either like or you don't. It'd probably be a bit better if it wasn't so wordy. The instrumentals are more like 3.5 but its like you have these great shoes but it comes with a mandatory stone inside you can't throw out. And as great as the shoes are... I might get used to it but why try when I can just get another pair.

If you want to hear working class music that actually reflects the views of the majority of the working class, go for this. It's funny how a lot (I'm not saying all) of militant left-wing stuff comes either from those in the middle class gone political or people who spend most of their time doing drugs, living in squats and being extremely proud of themselves for it (regardless of how you view such lifestyle it has nothing to do with the *working* class). The right-wing ideologues... well, there's no need to even comment on them. That being said, these are not songs by nihilists who don't care about anything. The music here is also not about being as in your face as possible,or being agressive, abrasive and "true". As many noted, these songs are very catchy, melodic, almost as if the Buzzcocks started playing oi! This is as wholesome and homey as punk can get.

It's easy to see why We Were Exploding Anyway is a controversial entry in 65daysofstatic's discography. It's a sizable departure from their signature sound, especially considering the album it followed up, The Destruction of Small Ideas. I felt that their approach to mixing and dynamics was commendable and unique on that project, especially given the loudness war that most music seems to be locked into these days. However, the timbre of the drums and guitars didn't mesh well together, and outside of a few tracks like Lyonesse, I felt that the tracks weren't really dynamic or ear-catching enough to be memorable.

Thankfully, that is nowhere near the case with We Were Exploding Anyway. In fact, almost every track on this project is an adrenaline-infused cacophony of frantic drum patterns, blaring synths, and noisy guitars. The previously subtle synths and electronic drums have been brought to the forefront of the mix, and several tracks completely abandon live instrumentation for significant lengths of time. This may come as a disappointment to post-rock fans, but to me, this makes We Were Exploding Anyway the most exciting and interesting album 65daysofstatic has released to date.

The album's opener, Mountainhead, kicks things off with a stilted 9/4 synthetic drum groove that soon gives way to a lovely guitar-backed build toward the end of the track. It's a really unique yet very catchy track, and I absolutely love how seamlessly the song flows from one idea to the next.

This transitions pretty seamlessly into Crash Tactics, another favorite of mine. It's really hard to separate the synthetic and acoustic drums on this track, lending a very unique array of sounds used in the breakneck drum pattern throughout the first half of the track. The jagged synth lead is used to great effect, too. The track just bleeds energy through its first half, until it heads into a drum-and-bass breakdown that explodes into a noisy guitar crescendo at the end of the track. It's very dynamic, especially in the incredible call-and-response between the drums and guitars at the end of the track.

I like Dance Dance Dance for similar reasons as Crash Tactics, though it does enough different to keep it from sounding like a retread of the same ideas. The gargantuan drums come out of nowhere, and mark a pretty sudden tonal shift in the track. Where Crash Tactics is energetic and lively, Dance Dance Dance is dark and unrelenting. That is, until the guitars open up the track near the end of the track in a rather triumphant-sounding finish.

Weak4 is another highlight with its frantic drum-and-bass groove opening up into a dynamic call-and-response melody later in the track. It might even be one of the most exciting tracks on the album, though I do think the drumline does repeat a bit too much.

Come To Me is unfortunately a pretty big misstep. Surprisingly, Robert Smith doesn't contribute much to the song. The lyrics are very repetitive, repeating some pretty meaningless phrases like "close your eyes" and "all you have to do is change your mind." His voice is pretty warbly and doesn't fit in very well with the melody in the instrumental. Luckily, though, 65daysofstatic comes through here with a pretty good instrumental, including a pretty neat breakdown at the midpoint of the song. The buildup toward the last verse is also very well done, and it's climactic enough to not kill the exciting pace of the album so far. I have no idea why this song needed to be 8 minutes, though.

Go Complex starts off pretty weak, as the vocoded vocal chops burst into a pretty cheesy synth loop and repetitive drumline. However, the sudden instrumental switchup at 2:00, when the guitars suddenly come in, is undeniably breathtaking.

The final two tracks, Debutante and Tiger Girl are pretty long-form buildups that bring a nice climax to the album. Debutante is especially pretty, with a really interesting processed drumline that repeats through much of the track. Tiger Girl is a bit patience-testing at the beginning, with its incredibly repetitive synth and drum patterns. There's something rather hypnotic about it, though, and given enough time, the track blossoms into a beautifully noisy finish once all of the guitars and acoustic drums are introduced.

When judged on its own merits, We Were Exploding Anyway is an inventive, dynamic, and beautiful addition to 65daysofstatic's discography, and is probably the most accessible for anyone not too sad to see 65 step outside of post-rock for a bit.

65daysofstatic at their most dreamy and sleepy.

One of the truly remarkable thing about 65daysofstatic's sound is that they never seem to stick to a particular sound. I was blown away by their last project, "We Were Exploding Anyway," even though that album received a lot of backlash from hardcore post-rockers. And I can see why -- the band's sudden turn to wild electronic experimentation was a really bizarre change of pace. Personally though, I loved the breakbeat grooves, the insane synth melodies, and incredible drumwork of tracks like Crash Tactics, Dance Dance Dance, and Debutante.

Critics of the last album might find this one to be a bit of a return to form. 65daysofstatic doesn't really abandon the heavy electronic instrumentation, but a lot of these tracks involve hypnotic, dreamy walls of sound led by some intriguing guitar layering, much like on 65daysofstatic's older work.

Personally, though, while this record brings a new, exciting direction to the band's sound, I found several of the tracks to be a bit sleepy for my taste, and the repetition in song structure gets pretty predictable after a while.

The album's opener, Heat Death Infinity Splitter, is a pretty good introduction to the band's new sound. It opens up with a pretty basic synth melody, but as the track goes on and on, more synths, guitars, and drums are slowly added to create a lovely wall of sound at the end. It's epic and awe-inspiring, even if it does take a little while to get into it.

Prisms is another awesome track from this album. It's mostly synth-led to begin with, but after a couple minutes, some acoustic drums fill in, and eventually some hypnotic guitar soundscapes make an appearance. I've always been impressed with 65daysofstatic's ability to keep a single song idea going throughout an entire track while still changing enough about the sound to keep it interesting. This track is a superb example of this, especially at the end as a more cohesive melody appears out of the noise.

While it's not one of my favorites, Blackspots is worth a mention. I love how the bass falls in and out of the drum groove, and how the layers of sound bleed into each other as the song progresses. I think the song might be trying to juggle a few too many ideas -- I don't really feel like I'm given enough time with each section to really appreciate it -- but the song definitely has an interesting flow and direction.

I'm not so sure why I wasn't so excited by The Undertow, Sleepwalk City, and Taipei. I can recognize them as having interesting drum grooves (Sleepwalk City especially) and neat guitar layering but beyond that, I don't feel like 65daysofstatic really pushes themselves much beyond their usual standard. In fact, Taipei feels like the most standard 65daysofstatic track I've heard. That's not really such a bad thing -- I still like all of these tracks -- but they kind of bog the middle of the album down a bit.

Unmake the Wild Light though. Hoooooollllyyyyy shit. This has to be my favorite 65dos track out of all of their projects. The somewhat ambient-but-still-unnerving intro gives way to a short bass-and-drum bridge that reminds me of some of my favorite tracks from their last project. This leads right back into the same groove as the intro, but as time goes on, the tension slowly rises and the whole track opens up into an incredible cacophony of guitars and pianos. 65daysofstatic really flexes their skill in song structure and slowly rising tension with this track.

Finally, Safe Passage finishes the whole project out with a nice noisy send-off. The first few minutes of the track are damn near quiet, but once the synths in the middle kick in, it's a really enjoyable track. I do wish it didn't end so suddenly, as I feel it leaves the album on a pretty sour note, but I feel like that may have been the artist's intention.

Overall, I really dig this project. I think that even though I prefer "We Were Exploding Anyway" as a cohesive album, a lot of my favorite 65daysofstatic tracks end up on "Wild Light." I'm excited to see what new sounds the band brings together for their next project.

As a disclaimer, I'd consider myself a big fan of Eric Andre's TV show and I've tried not to let that color my impression of this album. The question I've been repeatedly asking myself is that if I wasn't aware of who Eric Andre was, or if I wasn't acquainted with his absurd, maniacal comedy, would I still enjoy this as much as I do? And surprisingly, I think the answer is a resounding "yes."

Badass Bullshit Benjamin Buttons Butthole Assassin is probably some of the most creatively assembled instrumental hip-hop I've ever heard, and I honestly can't believe I just typed that sentence without a lick of irony. There's so many intricate pieces to this track that flow from one to the next as smooth as butter, and every single sample sounds absolutely excellent.

There's a TON of instrumental details I could point out about the rest of the album - the way the strings crescendo on Banana and then break down into the oddly chopped drum groove before fading out into oblivion then smoothly transitioning into yet another great drum pattern on Like That and then after barely 30 seconds switches to the wall of noisy guitar chords on I Dunno is this album at its best imo.

I feel this is essentially the antithesis of a common criticism of instrumental hip-hop albums in that some producers can make a nice 8 bars and loop it with minimal modification for 5 minutes. This album chucks out one insane idea after another after another, with barely any time to process anything before you're whisked away to the next 15-second snippet of madness. That's not gonna be everyone's thing but to me that's made this album infinitely replayable.

Except.

EXCEPT.

EXCEPT for I Worship Satan, which takes everything I just said in that last paragraph and completely reverses it. It's a nearly 13 minute noise piece. In the middle of the album. Now I dunno about y'all but this completely killed the incredible momentum of this album for me. It's a cool listen if you're into that kinda thing but I definitely would have enjoyed this album WAY more without half of its runtime being dominated by a 13-minute, ultimately kinda samey joke. (minus the ending, which I think is another highlight of the album) This track alone is why I'm giving a middling rating despite enjoying the hell out of every single other track. If this album is the aural equivalent of The Eric Andre Show then I Worship Satan would be the equivalent of interrupting an interview to have someone read poetry. It could be hilarious, and it could be well-written poetry, but I doubt they'd stretch that particular joke for 13 minutes.

And that brings me to my next point. This album is clearly a joke, verging on a shitpost. It's a funny joke - I actually think Eric Andre's particular style of absurd comedy transfers really well to this album - and for the most part I'm impressed with the fact that an absurd comedy album like this can still be enjoyed for the music alone. That part will be subjective of course, and I'll admit I'm kind of a sucker for this particular style of grungy, dissonant, wild hip-hop production. As a producer myself though I'm also just blown away at how technically proficient Eric Andre is, of all people.

So even if this doesn't seem like your kind of thing, I'd still recommend giving it a listen. It's a very unique project that I found equal parts puzzling and impressive. Bird the fuck up and hold onto your ranch.

column2: The Dandy Warhols - Why You So Crazy (2019)
column7:
This hurts.

I've admittedly got a bit of a soft spot for the Dandys. My introduction to the band, Thirteen Tales From Urban Bohemia is still one of my most-played albums ever, and even though after that point their discography becomes much more mediocre, I was pleasantly surprised by Distortland. I'm actually pretty sad that album was so heavily panned, since I think it shows a level of maturity and more succinct songwriting that I think the band lacked in prior releases. This is coupled with some of the best instrumentals I've heard the band come together with in a long time. Songs like Doves and Search Party were intoxicatingly dreamy, while Catcher in the Rye and STYGGO are absolutely lovely on the ears.

When I heard the first single to this album, Forever, it seemed like we were going to get some more of the same ideas that made Distortland great. The thin, weary vocals riding on top of the eerily dreamy instrumental are candy to my ears. I was incredibly excited for this album. All signs pointed to this being the Dandys' moment to prove themselves in their late career.

And... well, this wasn't it. In fact Forever is pretty much the only song I liked on the album. I think the band's attitude hasn't changed much from Distortland, so while I'd call this album well-intentioned, the ideas these songs are built around are nowhere near as strong as they were on prior work.

Terraform has some of the worst vocal effects I've heard in a while, and the obnoxiously repetitive drum pattern and bassline aren't any help. This is such a weak opener, which is surprising since previous Dandy Warhols albums generally featured excellent introductions. Godless, We Used To Be Friends, Search Party... I wish Terraform had half of the punch any of those songs had.

From there, the album continues by flipping between awkward acoustic rock and awkward experimental rock. Highlife was almost enjoyable, but the foot-stomping kick-clap drums mix with the buzzy electric guitar solos about as well as peanut butter and Vaseline. I wanted to love Thee Elegant Bum, both for its well-produced bouncy beat and its intentionally laughable title, but Courtney's vocals does not sound good at all here. I'd say it sounds like a bad Gorillaz B-side, but even their B-sides aren't this aimless.

To the Church and Motor City Steel, though, are definitely the worst songs here. To the Church starts off in an interesting-if-not-that-enjoyable way with the odd metallic synth bouncing off of the sequenced drums, but by the time the midpoint rolls around, the extra layered synths, acoustic AND electric guitars, weird choral pads, odd gong samples, and Courtney's shaky vocals come together in the most stomach-churning way. I appreciate the experimentation here, but good god, this does not sound good at all. Motor City Steel, meanwhile, is the polar opposite. It's so squeaky-clean that it sounds like music for a bubbly Ford commercial, and god damn it that 909 clap is so out of place that I can't stop hearing it. every. fucking. second. of. this. song.

This at least is followed by Forever, which as mentioned before, I love, even in the context of this album. It transitions smoothly into a piano outro, Ondine, which is out of place, but is at least pleasant. It's well-arranged and it's a good way to wind down from... whatever the hell just happened.

Overall, I'd say give this a miss unless you're a hardcore Dandy Warhols fan and want to hear them mash every single strange sound they were capable of producing together. Regardless of all of this, though, I still think the Dandy Warhols have some good material left in them. I'm at least glad to see they're not stagnating; in fact, this album suffers from crazy experimentation around somewhat poor ideas. I'm still a fan of these guys, and I'm definitely going to be checking out what they have next. All I hope is that they bring the same maturity and experimentation they've had on their last two releases to some better ideas.

Man, I was really hoping for something exceptional from these guys after their pretty awesome debut. Their first album didn't really push any boundaries but I loved it for how well-executed and catchy of a synthfunk album it was.

This time around, it seems Jungle was keen to experiment a bit, and that's kind of exactly what I wanted. In the end, though, I think this album's a bit of a mess because of it. The production seems a little more shoddy, with a lot of instruments drenched in this awful-sounding reverb that drowns out the actually pretty creative and groovy instrumentals. The vocal performances aren't quite as strong, either. They're a lot more dissonant and off-beat this time around, but it doesn't seem like they're quite meant to be. And I think this album lacks a definitive ear-grabber like Busy Earnin', Time, or Julia from their debut.

Gotta hand it to em though. Heavy, California and Beat 54 (All Good Now) are excellent. I love the epic progression of Mama Oh No, and Pray is a great closer. So there's some really great material here, but I don't think Jungle's sound came together as well this time around.

My favourite album by the 65s. More electronic and upbeat than anything else they've done (though still plenty of guitar action), this is infectiously groovy and bounds along at a breathless pace. Whilst being a great blend of stompy breakbeaty/idm stuff and the epic post-rocks, for me it transcends analysis, oozes positivity and is all about being totally lost in the moment...swept away by one of those big waves that life randomly throws at you.

Also, dat cover.
4.3*

Many good atmospheric tracks here but falls into the usual (avoidable) trap of remix albums - too many similar remixes of the same songs. In this case we have 15 remixes of only 5 unique tracks, and they're all grouped by source - so when the fourth version of Pearls2Swine in a row starts up, you're about to defenestrate the hifi. This is basically unlistenable as an album.

Why not choose some remixes of your other tracks, or choose the best and make an EP instead of an album? NO LOL WE LIEK REMIXEZ

Obviously there's the voice. Other than that...occasional flashes of purity and an impressive talent, for the most part swallowed up by the production and schmaltz. I prefer the big epic tracks like Set Fire to the Rain and Rolling in the Deep; if it's going to be overblown pop with a shiny production then I want it to be huge...really huge. The cover of Lovesong is too obvious and somewhat tedious when taken in the context of the other tracks; at this point in the album there is a substantial weary feeling induced by the simplistic lyrical themes, seemingly single-minded subject matter (just get over him already, girl) and clinical arrangements. This is no doubt a product of her age and pop producers, noting her raw talent, having assigned a target market, proceeding to squeeze as many sentimental ballads as possible into the album.

The album picks up at the end for the (thankfully) wonderfully stripped down Someone Like You, which is pretty devastating and probably the highlight here. I hope in a few years she'll have some more experiences to draw on and the ability to take more control of the writing process. She certainly could benefit a slightly more raw production, at the very least.
Ok, so I was wrong about Gaga. She's actually pretty decent as far as pop goes, and I don't find her singles anywhere near as irritating as I once did.

column2: Nine Inch Nails - With Teeth [Limited Tour Edition] (2005)
column7:
Certainly far from the best NIN release, but quite decent and has some good memorable tracks on it. This version has a bonus DVD with 5.1 mix of the album, and it lifts the music to the extent where one can't help but think that some of these tracks were written to be played on a surround system.

Whilst just falling short of essential listening, the surround version displays a mastery of the additional space, making most tracks (especially those with significant electronic sections) feel a lot less flat and anaemic, whilst providing an elevated sense of dynamics for the album as a whole. Highly recommended for NIN fans who have access to the necessary equipment.

3.7*

One of my favourite metallic film soundtracks. This is loud, cheesy, dumb and lots of fun. Even Coal Chamber manage to produce a track that is not only decent but works well with the album as a whole.

Some great moments spoilt somewhat by the vocals - especially the operatic stuff. For some idea of what this _could_ have been like, look no further than the ambient closer A Hand of Awful Rewards: certainly a bit one-dimensional when compared to the best ambient, but definitely a winner compared to the vocal-heavy tracks.

Regardless of the flaws here, it's good to see them trying something different.

3.1*

This is a strange one, I love post rock soundscapes and electronics noise. This was the first thing I have ever listened to by 65daysofstatic. As I had no pre-conception or prior knowledge of their earlier work, I loved it! It is experimental and very unique, sure some things don't really work, but good on you fellas for trying and letting us hear the results. I feel here in RYM, there is a sense of ownership and betrayal sometimes, this is unwarranted and projects nonsensical expectations on bands by their fans. Most bands need to evolve and it is good to listen to them do so. So for those about to post-rock we salute you!

life changing

12 years old, I went to the Leo superstore, bought this with my own cash......went home and put it on the record player.......been headbanging and buying music ever since, my heavily bias opinion, simply excellent, everyone should own this album.

Well I did try…

To start, I have to point out, I’m mortally scarred by Phil Colin’s unforgivable 80s tune-age. This was enhanced by sitting round a mate of mine’s house at 13-14 and being forced to listen to Genesis. I was utterly bored. Why can’t we put on some Motley Crue or Twisted Sister? Ok, I haven’t crowned myself in any glory here, I know, but at least it gives context to my prejudice, which I thought I had over come with age.

On hearing Phil Collins voice I am instantly irritated. Now that said, many a respected radio presenters have adoration for the lamb lies down and trick of the tail. So, I thought we’ll at least the very underrated Steve Hackett is in the band, let’s give it another whirl. Whilst browsing records at a car-boot, wind & wuthering was there for a couple of quid, and as this was their last fully prog outing. So why not. Well while the first two track are ok, I still live with my prejudices. Whilst I have grown fond of early 10cc, Phil Collins Genesis is never going to be my thing. That’s not to say it’s a bad album, clearly it’s not and there a many a fair folk that will pay testament to it’s accolades. Sadly not me. There is amazing musicianship at play her, which I appreciate. It just leaves me with nothing as a whole, apart from one for the vine. May be Phil in another life time.

Almost works, but not quite

To say that this is a terrible record would be harsh! It has something intangible that make you want to like the record, and for me is linked to the beats and samples which work. Ultimately however, this record ends up being a bit dull, and too repetitive, normally a good thing for a dance record. A bit of a shame!

Loving it!

I was expecting to be disappointed after pimp your butterfly's soaring heights, but god damn Mr Lamar, you have done it again! Different more commercial with slicker production doesn't detract from the beauty of this album...add to this Kendrick Lamar's ability to capture sentiment and feeling of not just himself but his wider audience sets him out from the crowd.
It's good if you're in the mood for it, otherwise, it overstays its welcome ten minutes in.

column2: Neutral Milk Hotel - In the Aeroplane Over the Sea (1998)
column7: I fucking love "Holland, 1945" but other than that I can't really place my finger on why this has been praised to hell and back. I don't hate it, I listened to it a fair share amount of times. Maybe I just don't get it.

There was a point where I considered myself a Psychobilly fan. But listening to two bands of the genres (this one and Tiger Army) does not warrant fandom in my opinion. I tried venturing into other Psychobilly, like the renowned Nekromantix, and well, I realized it wasn't to my liking. Still, this is a cult favorite of mine considering it reminds me of 2005 a lot. Whether I'm a fan of the genre or not, this album is still pretty incredible. It has some amazing vocal performances, sung by Vic Victor. Not to mention, the guitar in this work is absolutely incredible. I picked up the guitar the other day after not picking up for a few years and I automatically played the lick to Koffin Kat Rock. And the stand-up bass is absolutely driving. It's their most accessible record, even to people new to the genre. Fans of the band say this is still their best work, so give it a shot.

The most telling aspect of The Fame is that it documents Lady Gaga at the callow stage of her career when she was at a crossroads. In the late stages of the 00s, the party girl atmosphere permeated American radio. Lady Gaga, in an attempt to make it big, adhered to this shtick as well and as result, we are treated to such tracks like the popular lead single "Just Dance," "Boys Boys Boys," "Money Honey," and the eponymous track. About 90% of the album is bound to the party girl notion, to the point of ad nauseum. Add to the fact that some of the tracks didn't exactly exhibit Stefani Germanotta's true writing potential, and you're left with an album consisting of a good amount of forgettable tracks and its four unforgettable singles. It's always a turn off when I encounter an album such as this, just a vehicle for the singles. But, repeated listens have since made me realize two things. First and foremost, Gaga does have a knack for writing fun music and has limitless potential; However, these same fun tracks are often pinned together with worthless lyrics and you're left with the sizzle but no steak. But in the end, this isn't a bad thing, after all, this is Pop, you're not exactly expecting Mozartesque songwriting here. But the album's saving grace is its ultimate single, "Paparazzi," the song that hooked yours truly. This song truly shows just the amount of talent Gaga holds as compared to her other Pop contemporaries. Gaga manages to find some sadness and incorporates it into the song subtly. I've often professed that "Paparazzi" is a sad song, and having heard it played live three times already I can safely attest to this. There are so many emotions that run through the song, it is criminally underrated as far as music is concerned. Both "LoveGame" and "Poker Face" are at this point iconic whether it is for their lyrics or for their very distinguishable synth hooks. Yet, the blatant sexual connotations tied to both songs always leave a sour taste in my mouth.Perhaps all her songs may have sexual connotations, but I feel it is in these songs where it is truly excessive.

Nonetheless, just four years later, and The Fame sounds completely dull and dated. With the advent of dubstep, production values have increased tenfold, leaving this collecting dust in our CD bins. It's not secret her popularity is waning at this point and it makes you realize just what made her special in the first place.

2002 was a simpler time. Facebook and Twitter were still years to come. Cell phones were around, but the outrageous price plans made you not only resort to using it when absolutely necessary but also made you resort to communicate physically (the dark ages man, I tell ya.) And Avril Lavigne's safer than Elmer's glue pop/rock was burning up the charts. Ah yes, what a simpler time, when Mtv was still about music (well, that is if you count Slipknot, Linkin Park and Limp Bizkit as music), when P2P sites weren't declared public enemy number one by the president himself. Hell, in 02 our president probably couldn't even turn on a computer, much less use the internet (stick your Twitter account up your ass, Senor Obama.) But damn, now I'm just rambling on, just like Avril does after track 4. "You mean I have to fill up a whole CD? But I have nothing to fill it up with, just like I have nothing to fill up the pockets of my totally rad cargo pants! Well, I do have some crude demos lying around, I even rap in one of them, LOL! Whaf does LOL mean you ask? It means 'laughing out loud,' I learned it in an AOL Chatroom last week. What's a chatroom? Oh, brother!"

Gosh darn it Two Thousand and Two, I miss you.

I always liked the neo-New Order vibe that I personally found in this album. But there were just so many things that drove me away from this album. For one, I never liked his voice. Secondly, it just seemed like masturbation, whether it be musical, lyrical or hell, even creative. It always came off as pretentious and that's really saying something considering I've heard worse albums.

I don't like this new one. I support the progression and sound changes in the bands, but We Were Exploding Anyway is a letdown for me. I mean, c'mon, it sounds like a Trance album for moments... and I'm a sucker for the Post-Rock genre, so don't expect hearing any guitar-driven and high-pitched atmospheres like their past releases. What we got here is a predominant electronic influence with hints of clean guitars in the background, and a distorted bass that reminds me of Russian Circles (and that's a good thing). But the excessive use of electronics kinda killed it for me. I guess it's a matter of tastes, you have to give it a try and like/dislike this new sound. If you ask me, The Destruction of Small Ideas is still their weakest effort to date.

column2: Explosions in the Sky - The Earth Is Not a Cold Dead Place (2003)
column7: A couple of years ago I was very apathetic towards this Texan band. I tried this album and really didn't care for it for many months. The first listen gave me no feelings at all and it left me wondering why many post-rock aficionados enjoyed this thing. I was beginning to think 'did these post-rockers need another gem in their genre other than Godspeed You! Black Emperor and Slint, so they had to choose a good modern post-rock album and decided this was the best the genre could get at that time? because I can't hear anything but "twinkletwinkletwinkletwinkle" guitars, marching drums and a simple bassline!' damn I was wrong. The simplicity of this album is definitely its strongest point. Oh, and the beauty of it, of course. Those simple chords helped with loads of reverb and delay create this beautiful sound that made me teary eyed more than once upon the second listen. Yes, you can call me a wimp for crying to Memorial and Your Hand In Mine (I'm especially refering to this track, which I consider one of the best, most moving tracks made by humankind), but I have to thank these guys for making me feel what a few albums could achieve. That is, complete sadness and joy at the same time. Nevertheless, whenever I listen to these tunes, I'm left with a feeling of hope and cheerfulness. Then I can confirm that this record is an emotional rollercoaster that can get you thinking and extract you from reality for less than an hour. How many bands can do that? And who on Earth needs lyrics, by the way?

column2: Godspeed You! Black Emperor - "No Title as of 13 February 2024 28,340 Dead" (2024)
column7:
My first time listening to this album was during a walk around the city the other day, which is not something I usually do with new releases. I prefer to listen to them at night, on my own, isolated if possible. This time, though, it didn't really make a difference because I knew that it'd not be something special like it often happened in the past with this band, so I went for it nevertheless.

It really didn't do much for me, and it confirmed my suspicions. GY!BE, since their comeback, has sounded very same-y, to my dismay, since I am (was?) a big fan of the band and their previous works. But ever since their comeback, well... their quality has been going down noticeably, and I can't turn a blind eye on it anymore.

'Allelujah! Don't Bend! Ascend! was the last true, full-blown GY!BE experience I can recall. They stuck to that sound and tone after it, and there's nothing wrong with that, but it doesn't do anything for me anymore. Efrim's and Mike's guitar tones have had the same sound ever since, and that's where the same-y adjective comes in full-force. Like other reviewers said, they have been repeating this crescendo formula that goes nowhere ever since, and it worries me. Yes, the buildups are there for sure, and there are good moments here and there, but the explosion never comes. That's a bummer in my book, and it's like they have become a copy of themselves at this point. Look, this is even coming from a guy who likes crescendocore and even encourages it if there's nothing else to expect from it but that; but this is freaking Godspeed we're talking about! And the music here would be fine for a run-of-the-mill post-rock outfit, but not them. It's like the magic is gone, man, and I don't think it's nostalgia speaking this time. I really feel like it's gone for good at this point. I also think that they released this record just for the sake of making a statement, which is fine, too, but again, Yanqui and Zero Kanada are ten times better than this, and they made a statement as well.

If you don't expect anything out-of-this-world from a post-rock record in the late 2024, fine! Take a listen, and you might (you will!) enjoy it! But to me, it feels like this record goes nowhere, and all of the building up just falls flat if we compare it to the rest of the catalogue of this monolithic band.
